structure.title: Genesis–Deuteronomy · A family becomes a people with obligations
structure.text: Creation and flood give way to households marked by promises, rivalries and migrations. Exodus expands a family story into deliverance from slavery. In the wilderness, story and law alternate as a people learn what their new freedom will require of them and of their descendants.

structure.title: Joshua–Esther · Living in the land, losing it, remembering it
structure.text: Settlement, kingship, division, exile and return receive accounts written from different points of view. Chronicles returns to ground already covered in Samuel and Kings. Meeting a king twice gives a reader the chance to see which ancestors, institutions or failures each account brings forward.

structure.title: Job–Song of Solomon · Suffering gets more than one voice
structure.text: A sufferer disputes with his friends, worshippers bring accusations and gratitude into song, and teachers weigh the promises and disappointments of daily life. A friend's confident speech in Job has a different standing from a narrator's account of what actually happened.

structure.title: Isaiah–Malachi · Hear a crisis as an argument
structure.text: Prophetic books address rulers, cities and exiles through accusations, laments, visions and promises. Their placement after the histories can obscure how often they speak back into the crises those earlier books recount. A restoration promised to people in exile has an address as well as a future.

structure.title: Matthew–Acts · Four tellings and an expanding circle
structure.text: Four Gospels tell of Jesus with different openings, emphases and arrangements. Acts follows the movement from Jerusalem into a wider Mediterranean world, where disputes about meals, circumcision and membership test what it means for people of different backgrounds to share a community.

structure.title: Romans–Revelation · Letters arrive, then a vision
structure.text: Letters deal with named communities and their quarrels, bereavements, collections and questions about worship. Revelation begins by addressing churches too, then turns to visions whose beasts, thrones and transformed city draw on a vocabulary the prophets have already given the reader.

people.name: Abraham and Sarah
people.text: The prospect of descendants is announced to a couple for whom having a child seems impossible. Their responses make trust, impatience and injury matters of family history long before later writers argue about what Abraham's faith means.

people.name: Moses
people.text: He stands between a people remembering slavery and the God who has delivered them. In one passage he transmits a demand. In another he argues on the people's behalf. Those different tasks give the wilderness story some of its most charged conversations.

people.name: Jesus
people.role: The central figure of four Gospels
people.text: Each Gospel places particular words, deeds and encounters around his death and resurrection. Holding the four tellings beside one another lets a reader follow what a parable, a sign or a question does in the company this evangelist has given it.

people.name: Paul
people.role: A letter writer answering communities at a distance
people.text: Rumours, reports and questions often reach Paul before his reader hears a word. Positions he quotes can belong to his correspondents. His shifts from argument to plea, practical instruction or greeting give clues about the relationship behind the letter.

context.title: Which collection is this?
context.text: This edition follows the Protestant ordering of the King James Bible. Jewish and other Christian collections arrange or include books differently. The sequence in front of you can shape expectations about what a book is leading toward, especially at the boundary between the two Testaments.

context.title: A covenant leaves traces in later arguments
context.text: Agreements and promises bind people across generations. A prophet accusing a city, a psalm asking for rescue and a letter discussing Abraham can each appeal to an earlier relationship. The force of the appeal depends partly on who made the promise and to whom.

notice.text: Identify the speaker before treating a verse as a conclusion.
notice.why: A king's boast, a friend's accusation, a psalmist's cry and a narrator's judgment can sound equally authoritative when detached from the page. Restoring the person and the occasion often changes the whole force of the words.

notice.text: Listen for the earlier event inside a later prayer.
notice.why: A crossing of water or a release from captivity can recur as something worshippers ask God to do again. Memory in these passages gives people words for a danger whose outcome they do not know.

notice.text: Notice when an argument turns into a meal.
notice.why: Passover, wilderness food, Jesus eating with outsiders and disputes at a shared table give belonging a visible form. The question of who gets fed, by whom and beside whom carries meaning a statement of doctrine can leave abstract.

opening: A brother kills his brother. A people escapes slavery and begins quarrelling in the wilderness. A righteous man loses everything and demands an answer from God. Centuries later, a teacher tells his listeners to love their enemies, and is executed. The Bible gathers stories, laws, songs, accusations, and promises that have given generations their language for suffering and hope. Read together, these writings are more unruly than their familiar quotations suggest: even the faithful argue, and some of the fiercest arguments are addressed to God.
